title: Shemini: be holy (Leviticus 11:44–45)
hookLine: the food laws end with a call: "be holy, for I am holy"

cards: Open a pantry in an observant Jewish home and look at the labels: small symbols on the cans and boxes, a U in a circle, a K, a star. Each one says an inspector checked what's inside. It can look like bookkeeping.

But those symbols trace back to a long chapter of Leviticus that lists which animals may be eaten: land animals that chew the cud and have split hooves, fish with fins and scales, and a long roll call of birds that may not be eaten.
At the end of all that detail, the chapter stops listing, and gives the reason.

teach.h: THE LIST ENDS WITH A REASON.
teach.b: After the animals, the reason comes: "ye shall therefore be holy, for I am holy." The food laws don't end on hygiene or health. They end on holiness.
The word is kadosh, holy. Its root, k-d-sh, means set apart, marked off for something.

You already know the family: kiddush, the blessing over wine that sets Shabbat apart from the week; kaddish, the prayer that sanctifies God's name; kiddushin, the word for marriage, two people set apart for each other.
Holy, in Hebrew, is less a glow than a boundary drawn with care. And look where this boundary is drawn. Not only in the sanctuary, where Shemini began, with fire and priests and an eighth day.
The chapter ends at the dinner plate. What you eat, three times a day, becomes a place where holiness happens.

Commentators have offered many reasons for the specific rules, and the Torah itself gives none beyond this one. Many Jews keep kashrut without needing a further reason: it's how they say yes to the call.

teach.h: BE HOLY, FOR I AM HOLY.
teach.b: Jewish practice wraps a meal in blessings, one before and another after, and the rabbis said a table can be like an altar. You don't have to keep kosher to notice what the chapter is doing.
It takes the most ordinary act there is, and says: here, too.

how: Many Jews keep kashrut, the dietary laws drawn from Leviticus 11 and later rabbinic law, and say a blessing before eating and Birkat Hamazon, the grace after meals, after a meal with bread.

o: holy: set apart for something that matters
kosher: fit to eat under Jewish law
pure: clean enough to bring to the altar

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: the sign of a kosher fish

s: Leviticus 11 explains the food laws as a health code
the chapter's own reason is holiness: be holy, for I am holy.
kadosh comes from a root meaning set apart
k-d-sh: marked off for something. kiddush and kiddushin share it.
land animals need split hooves and must chew the cud

games.q: the chapter lists animals, fish and birds in detail. how does it end?
o: with a call to be holy.
games.why: be holy, for I am holy. the long list turns out to be about holiness at the dinner table.

practice: Picture the next thing you'll eat: where it grew, and who carried it, cooked it, packed it. When the meal comes, take the first three bites slowly, with no screen.
Many Jews say a blessing before eating; if you pray, say one you know, and if not, a moment of noticing is its own kind of setting apart.

wordCard.voice: Kadosh. Holy: set apart, marked off for something that matters. The root of kiddush, kaddish and kiddushin.

orig.note: Hebrew: holy, set apart. root k-d-sh, as in kiddush, kaddish and kiddushin.

carryVoice: Your line: holy in the everyday. Even a dinner plate can be set apart. See you tomorrow.
